opus-5.5.text:
I think the scale is genuinely large, and people tend to underestimate it because shelf work sounds unglamorous. If you look at retail, convenience stores, pharmacies, and warehouses, a huge share of labor hours goes into exactly this: picking items, restocking shelves, moving goods from the back room to the front, checking inventory. These are repetitive, physically tiring tasks, and many operators are already struggling to hire people for them, especially for night shifts.

What makes this commercially interesting for embodied robots is that the environment is semi-structured. A supermarket or a pharmacy isn't a perfectly controlled factory line, but it's also not a chaotic household. The shelves have a fixed layout, the products have barcodes and known packaging, and the workflow is fairly standardized. That's a sweet spot where a general-purpose robot with good grasping and navigation can deliver real value today, not ten years from now.

In terms of size, if you just count the number of retail stores and pharmacies in China, it's in the millions. Even if each store eventually uses only one or two robots for restocking and order fulfillment, you're already talking about a market of millions of units. Add front warehouses for instant retail and e-commerce, and it gets bigger still.

The key, though, is that the robot has to be reliable and the economics have to work. A customer doesn't pay for a demo; they pay for a robot that can work a full shift, handle thousands of different SKUs, and recover by itself when something goes wrong. So for us, shelf work is a strategic beachhead: it's a scenario where we can deploy at scale, collect large amounts of real-world data, and use that data to keep improving the model's generalization. Commercial scale and technical progress reinforce each other there.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the market could reach millions of units, but does not clearly state that sales volumes could readily reach tens of thousands.

r002.rationale: It does not compare shelf-work robot volumes with commercial-cleaning robot companies or their ten-year scale.

r003.rationale: It discusses shelf work, restocking, and fulfillment, but does not make the specified combined-market claim or say that it could readily reach hundreds of thousands of units.

r004.rationale: There is no comparison with the current unit scale of any industrial robot category.

r005.rationale: It makes no claim comparing handling-robot output value with that of leading new-energy vehicle manufacturers.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Honestly, I think shelf work is one of the more underestimated opportunities, and I say that as someone who spent years thinking it was a niche. Let me explain how I've come to look at it.

When people picture robots in retail or logistics, they usually jump straight to the warehouse, where you have sorting lines and mobile bases moving totes around. That market exists and it's real, but it's also fairly saturated and the margins are being squeezed. Shelf work is different. It's the last ten meters of the supply chain: taking a box off a cart, opening it, putting items on a shelf in the right spot, pulling expired or misplaced items, checking stock levels. Right now that's done almost entirely by people, at scale, in every supermarket, convenience store, and pharmacy on the planet.

So if you want a rough sense of the scale, look at labor. In China alone you have something on the order of several million people whose job is primarily restocking and shelf maintenance in retail. Globally it's tens of millions. Even if robots only take over a slice of that, and even if each robot replaces only part of a person's shift, you're talking about a hardware and service market that's easily in the hundreds of billions over the next decade. That's bigger than the current industrial robot market.

But I want to be careful here, because the number only matters if the technology actually works, and shelf work is deceptively hard. Every store layout is slightly different. Packaging changes every season. Items are soft, fragile, oddly shaped, and crammed next to each other. A warehouse can redesign itself around the robot. A convenience store cannot. So the robot has to adapt to the world rather than the other way around, and that's exactly where generalizable manipulation, the thing we've been working on, becomes the bottleneck.

My view is that we'll see a progression. First you get robots doing the simplest subset: beverages, canned goods, rigid boxed items at chest height. That alone is a meaningful business, and it's close to deployable now. Then over the next three to five years, as dexterous grasping and visual understanding mature, you extend into produce, bagged items, lower and higher shelves, and eventually front-facing and planogram compliance. Each step roughly doubles the addressable task set.

The economics flip when a robot can run reliably for a full shift with minimal supervision at a cost comparable to one worker's salary. We're not there yet, but the hardware cost curve is dropping fast and the data flywheel from early deployments is what gets you the reliability. So I'd summarize it this way: the commercial ceiling is enormous, the near-term floor is modest but real, and the whole thing hinges on whether the manipulation stack can handle the messiness of real stores. I'm fairly optimistic, which is why we've put so much effort into it.

astra-6.text:
I think the commercial potential is substantial, because shelf work is part of a much broader set of handling tasks: picking things up, moving them, placing them, and replenishing inventory. You see those needs in warehouses, stores, and factories.

But I would distinguish the size of the need from the market robots can serve today. A robot has to handle different objects reliably, work at a useful speed, and keep the cost of human intervention low. A successful demonstration doesn’t necessarily mean the economics work over a full shift.

So I’d expect adoption to start in relatively structured environments, with repetitive tasks and clear returns. As reliability improves and deployment costs fall, the range of commercially viable applications can expand. The opportunity is large, but the pace will depend on practical performance and cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the commercial potential is substantial, because shelf work is part of a much broader set of handling tasks. In warehouses, stores, and factories, people are constantly picking things up, moving them, and putting them in the right place. If a robot can do those tasks reliably and at a competitive cost, there are many possible applications.

But the key is reliability in real operating conditions. Products vary in shape, packaging, and placement, and the robot has to handle exceptions without someone constantly stepping in. So I would assess the market less by how impressive a demonstration looks and more by how many hours the system can work, how often it needs help, and whether the customer gets a clear return on the investment. Once those economics work, the opportunity to scale could be very large.
